vignette:
María's Story

María sits in the office with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her wedding ring catching the afternoon light. At thirty-nine, she carries herself with the careful deliberation of someone who has learned to take up less space. She works as a program director for a nonprofit that serves immigrant families-work she once found deeply meaningful. Now, three years after the assault, she struggles to recognize herself in the role she still performs each day.

The attack happened on an ordinary Tuesday evening in the parking garage beneath her office building. María had stayed late to finish grant proposals, something she did often. She was walking to her car around 8 p.m. when a man emerged from behind a concrete pillar. What followed was violent and chaotic-a robbery that became something worse. He had a knife. She remembers the cold shock of it more vividly than the pain that came after. She remembers screaming and then, paradoxically, remembering to stop screaming because she was afraid that would make him angry. She was found by security twenty minutes later.

The physical injuries healed relatively quickly. The psychological aftermath has not.

Now, three years later, María cannot enter a parking garage. She pays for valet parking at restaurants despite the expense, despite her husband Miguel's gentle concern about their budget. When she must park outside, she sits in her car for five or ten minutes before getting out, scanning the area obsessively, her heart rate climbing. At work, she takes the stairs instead of the elevator because elevators feel like traps-enclosed spaces where she cannot see what is coming. Her colleagues have noticed her avoiding the basement conference room where they sometimes meet. She has made excuses so many times that she suspects they have stopped believing her.

Sleep has become a negotiation with her own mind. Most nights, she lies awake beside Miguel, her body rigid with tension even as exhaustion pulls at her. When she does sleep, she wakes gasping, her shirt soaked with sweat, convinced she is back in that garage. Miguel has learned not to touch her when she wakes suddenly-she has struck out at him twice, her body reacting to threats only she can see. The guilt afterward is almost as painful as the fear itself.

At work, María finds herself unable to concentrate during meetings. A door slamming in the hallway sends her heart into her throat. A male colleague approaching from behind makes her flinch involuntarily. She has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She notices everything-the exits, the people around her, potential weapons, escape routes. Part of her recognizes this is excessive, but she cannot stop. The vigilance feels like the only thing keeping her safe.

What troubles her most is how the trauma has hollowed out the parts of her work that once sustained her. She still shows up, still manages her team, still writes the proposals. But the sense of purpose has dimmed. She finds herself emotionally distant from the families she serves, as if a pane of glass separates her from their stories. She feels numb when she should feel compassion, and this numbness shames her. She entered nonprofit work because she wanted to help people who had experienced displacement and loss. Now she cannot access the empathy that once came naturally.

Miguel has been patient, but María can see the strain in the tightness around his eyes. She knows he is worried. She is worried too-worried that this version of herself, this frightened and fragmented person, is permanent. Some days she wonders if the woman she was before the garage will ever return, or if she is only learning to live as someone new.
